questionText: What is a device driver's main role?
options: Compile all user programs
Store the complete directory tree in CPU registers
Choose every application's password
Translate OS I/O requests into device-specific operations
explanation: Drivers bridge generic operating-system interfaces and particular device hardware or protocols.

questionText: What does a device controller typically provide?
options: Hardware registers or interfaces for commands, status and transfers
Only high-level application menus
A separate user account for each byte
The filesystem's entire naming policy
explanation: The CPU and driver communicate with the controller through a defined device interface.

questionText: What can the CPU do while waiting for an interrupt-driven I/O request to finish?
options: Necessarily poll the device continuously
Stop every process for the whole transfer
Assume completion before receiving any status
Execute other runnable work
explanation: Completion interrupts avoid requiring the CPU to spend the entire wait actively checking the device.

questionText: Why use a memory buffer during I/O?
options: Accommodate differences in transfer rate, size or timing
Eliminate all data copies in every design
Remove the need for error checking
Make every device infinitely fast
explanation: Buffers decouple producers and consumers that operate at different rates or in different units.

questionText: Which operation is characteristic of a block device interface?
options: Always execute a shell command per byte
Read or write addressed fixed-size storage blocks
Assign process priorities
Only consume an unaddressed stream of keypresses
explanation: Block interfaces support addressable transfer units such as logical blocks on storage devices.

questionText: Which device is commonly exposed using a stream-oriented character interface?
options: A terminal
A CPU page table
A virtual-memory frame allocator
A filesystem block bitmap itself
explanation: Character interfaces commonly present streams rather than randomly addressed storage blocks.

questionText: Why provide a uniform OS read/write interface across many devices?
options: All devices must use the same speed
No device driver is needed anymore
Applications need less device-specific control code
Every device then has identical physical behavior
explanation: A common interface abstracts differences while drivers handle hardware-specific details and limitations.

questionText: Why should a program check the result of an I/O operation?
options: The operation may fail or transfer fewer bytes than requested
The return value is always the user's PID
Errors necessarily erase every disk
All I/O calls always succeed fully
explanation: Resource limits, device faults and interruption can lead to errors or partial transfers.

questionText: What distinguishes asynchronous I/O submission from a blocking read?
options: The operation never reports completion
The data is always ready before submission begins
The device no longer needs a controller
Submission can return before the I/O completes
explanation: Completion is reported later through the relevant event, callback or result mechanism.

questionText: What does memory-mapped I/O make accessible through address-space operations?
options: Only ordinary executable files
Device control or data registers
A guarantee of cacheable device accesses
Every remote user's private memory
explanation: Specific physical address ranges are decoded as device interfaces; access rules may differ from normal RAM.

questionText: What is rotational latency on a rotating disk?
options: Waiting for a process to authenticate
Waiting for the target sector to rotate under the head
Translating a virtual address
Moving a file into a directory
explanation: It is distinct from seek time, which moves the head to the appropriate track.

questionText: Which HDD cost is absent from an SSD's normal data access mechanism?
options: Mechanical head seek time
All transfer time
All possible queue delay
All controller processing
explanation: SSDs have no rotating platter or moving read/write head, although electronic and software latency remain.

questionText: At a sustained 100 MB/s, how long does transferring 20 MB take, ignoring all overhead and using decimal units?
options: 5 s
2 s
explanation: Time equals data divided by rate: 20/100=0.2 seconds.

questionText: A disk rotates at 7200 RPM. Assuming a uniformly random sector angle, what is average rotational latency?
options: About 8.33 ms
About 60 ms
About 4.17 ms
About 0.417 ms
explanation: One turn takes 60/7200 seconds=8.33 ms; average waiting is half a rotation, about 4.17 ms.

questionText: A request needs 5 ms seek, 3 ms rotational wait and 2 ms transfer, with no queueing. What is total service time?
options: 7 ms
8 ms
10 ms
30 ms
explanation: The specified serial components add: 5+3+2=10 ms.

questionText: How can double buffering improve an I/O pipeline?
options: One buffer can be processed while the other is filled
It guarantees twice the speed in every workload
It makes both buffers the same physical bytes
It eliminates synchronization requirements
explanation: Overlap can reduce idle periods if device and CPU work can proceed independently.

questionText: Why must the CPU and a DMA-capable device coordinate buffer lifetime?
options: Freeing memory automatically cancels every hardware transaction
DMA always completes synchronously at function entry
A device cannot write memory
The device may still access the buffer after CPU submission returns
explanation: Reusing or freeing a buffer too early can corrupt memory or expose unrelated data.

questionText: On a non-coherent DMA system, why are cache-maintenance operations sometimes needed?
options: Device memory can never hold application data
DMA automatically invalidates all caches on every architecture
CPU caches and device-visible memory may contain different versions
Caches exist only on disks
explanation: The driver must follow platform rules so each participant sees the intended data before and after ownership transfer.

questionText: What is a major purpose of an IOMMU for device DMA?
options: Translate and restrict device-visible memory addresses
Increase a disk's mechanical rotation rate
Store every file's name
Choose the next user process by priority
explanation: Device address translation and access isolation limit what a DMA-capable device can reach.

questionText: Why might a device combine several completion notifications into fewer interrupts?
options: Remove the need to process completion records
Make transfer errors impossible
Reduce per-event CPU overhead at a possible latency cost
Guarantee zero queueing delay
explanation: Coalescing amortizes interrupt handling but can delay notification of individual completions.

questionText: Why can additional outstanding requests improve SSD throughput up to a point?
options: More requests always reduce each request's latency
Queueing removes all controller overhead
An SSD has infinitely many independent channels
They expose device parallelism and hide per-request latency
explanation: Concurrency can utilize internal resources, though excessive depth can increase queueing delay.

questionText: Why can shortest-seek-time-first starve some HDD requests?
options: The farthest request is always chosen first
Every request must be served within one seek
A continuing stream of nearby requests can postpone a far request
All pending cylinders are identical
explanation: Optimizing immediate seek distance does not itself guarantee bounded waiting.

questionText: What distinguishes SCAN from LOOK in classic disk scheduling?
options: SCAN travels to an endpoint; LOOK reverses at the last pending request in that direction
LOOK always visits both physical endpoints
SCAN chooses the nearest request regardless of direction
LOOK serves requests only in arrival order
explanation: Both sweep, but LOOK avoids travel beyond the furthest currently pending request.

questionText: Why can circular SCAN offer more uniform waiting than servicing both directions?
options: It ignores cylinder positions entirely
Every request is served immediately on arrival
Requests are served in one sweep direction before wrapping
The head never moves between requests
explanation: A single service direction reduces the directional asymmetry of requests waiting near opposite ends.

questionText: A nonblocking read has no available data but the stream has not ended. What is an appropriate outcome on UNIX?
options: Permanent deletion of the device
A false claim that a full buffer was read
An EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK-style error
Mandatory process termination
explanation: Nonblocking mode avoids sleeping for data; lack of data is distinct from EOF.

questionText: Why must code still handle a would-block result after a readiness notification?
options: The descriptor becomes a regular file automatically
Another consumer or state change may remove readiness before the operation
Readiness notifications always contain the full data payload
Ready means no operation can ever fail
explanation: Readiness is an observation of state, not an irrevocable reservation of data for that caller.

questionText: What should a bounded I/O pipeline do when its consumer cannot keep up?
options: Allocate unlimited memory forever
Apply backpressure or an explicit bounded overflow policy
Increase the producer's privilege level
Silently claim all data was consumed
explanation: Bounded queues require controlling production or defining intentional dropping/error behavior under overload.

questionText: What is the main redundancy property of two-disk RAID 1 with complete mirrored copies?
options: Both disks can fail without data loss guaranteed
It provides twice the raw usable capacity
It replaces the need for backups against deletion
One disk can fail while a surviving copy remains
explanation: Mirroring duplicates data for device-failure tolerance; it does not protect against all logical corruption or mistakes.

questionText: Four equal 1 TB disks form RAID 5. Ignoring metadata and using decimal capacity, what usable capacity is typical?
options: 1 TB
3 TB
2 TB
4 TB
explanation: Distributed single-parity protection uses capacity equivalent to one disk, leaving (4-1)×1=3 TB.

questionText: A stable I/O system averages 200 requests/s and 0.01 s total time per request. By Little's law, what is average requests in the system?
explanation: L=λW=200×0.01=2 requests, including both waiting and service under the stated system boundary.

questionText: Why can batching improve throughput yet worsen individual request latency?
options: A batch makes each device physically faster by definition
Throughput and latency are mathematically identical
Batches eliminate every per-request delay
Batch formation and shared processing amortize overhead but add waiting
explanation: Per-batch work can be cheaper per request while early arrivals wait for the batch or its scheduled processing.

questionText: Why might an I/O scheduler merge adjacent storage requests?
options: Guarantee no storage request ever fails
Make nonadjacent blocks physically identical
Reduce command overhead and exploit sequential transfer efficiency
Remove the need to complete each caller's request
explanation: Merging can reduce setup cost, but completion and error accounting must still preserve each request's semantics.

questionText: Why can canceling asynchronous I/O require waiting for a cancellation/completion result before reusing its buffer?
options: The operation may already be executing or completing
Buffer ownership is unrelated to I/O lifetime
The device must be idle whenever the API returns
Cancellation always rolls back device writes instantly
explanation: Cancellation is often a request, not immediate proof that all device accesses have stopped.

questionText: A read fails a checksum check. Why should the driver not simply return the corrupted bytes as a successful read?
options: Every checksum mismatch is harmless
Applications cannot observe read results
Checksums only affect file names
Callers need a reliable error/recovery signal rather than silently invalid data
explanation: Integrity failures should follow the device and OS error-handling protocol, which may include retries or recovery.

questionText: A pipeline has a 400 MB/s device and a 100 MB/s bus carrying all its data. Ignoring overhead, what bounds end-to-end throughput?
options: 100 MB/s
400 MB/s
500 MB/s
300 MB/s
explanation: A serial pipeline cannot exceed its slowest required stage; here the bus limits the rate to 100 MB/s.

questionText: What does scatter-gather support allow a device to transfer?
options: The CPU's entire register file without permission
Every file on every mounted filesystem
Data described by multiple memory-region descriptors
Only one physically contiguous application buffer in every case
explanation: A descriptor list identifies multiple regions, reducing the need to coalesce them into one contiguous buffer.

questionText: The head starts at cylinder 50 moving upward. Pending requests are 10,40,60,90. Under LOOK, with no new arrivals, what total movement serves all requests?
options: 80 cylinders
120 cylinders
140 cylinders
180 cylinders
explanation: The path is 50→60→90→40→10: movement 10+30+50+30=120. LOOK reverses at 90, not the physical endpoint.

questionText: The head starts at 50 moving upward; requests are 10,40,60,90. Under C-LOOK, counting wrap movement, what total movement serves all requests?
options: 150 cylinders
200 cylinders
120 cylinders
80 cylinders
explanation: Service path is 50→60→90→10→40. Including wrap gives 10+30+80+30=150 cylinders.

questionText: Cylinders are 0–199. Head starts at 50 moving upward; requests are 10,40,60,90. SCAN reaches 199 before reversing and stops once all requests finish. What movement occurs?
options: 388 cylinders
338 cylinders
120 cylinders
298 cylinders
explanation: The head travels 199-50=149 cylinders upward, then 199-10=189 to the last request, totaling 338.

questionText: A pipeline transfers each chunk in 5 ms and processes it in 8 ms. With perfect two-stage overlap after startup, what steady-state chunk interval is possible?
options: 3 ms
5 ms
8 ms
13 ms
explanation: The slower stage limits steady-state throughput, so the interval is max(5,8)=8 ms; initial fill/drain costs still apply.

questionText: An adapter completes 12000 requests/s. One interrupt per request costs 5 microseconds. If groups of 6 use one interrupt of the same cost, what CPU time per second is saved?
options: 5 ms
50 ms
60 ms
10 ms
explanation: Without batching: 12000×5=60000 microseconds. With groups: 2000×5=10000. Savings are 50000 microseconds=50 ms per second.

questionText: In a classic small RAID-5 read-modify-write update of one data block, which four block operations are commonly needed?
options: Write four complete mirrored copies of all data
Read old data and parity, then write new data and parity
Read only the new data four times
Read four directory names
explanation: Updating parity from the data difference typically requires two old-block reads and two new-block writes, absent cache or full-stripe optimizations.

questionText: Why may a storage flush or force-unit-access command matter after the OS submits a write?
options: All write caches are permanently powered by definition
A device may acknowledge data held only in volatile write-back cache
Flushing changes the file's owner
Device acknowledgment always proves physical durability
explanation: Durability requires commands and hardware that honor persistence semantics through relevant caches.

questionText: Why must a driver quiesce DMA and synchronize pending completions before freeing its queues?
options: Freeing a queue automatically resets every bus master
Queues contain no addresses
Interrupt handlers cannot overlap device removal
Otherwise hardware or callbacks can access freed memory
explanation: Teardown must end asynchronous access before releasing memory and objects used by those accesses.

questionText: A device can finish one request every 2 ms. Requests arrive steadily at 600/s. Ignoring drops, can its queue remain stable indefinitely?
options: No; capacity is only 2/s
Yes; any finite arrival rate is stable
Yes; CPU priority removes device service time
No; capacity is 500/s, below arrival rate
explanation: The maximum service rate is 1000/2=500 requests/s. Arrivals exceed capacity by 100/s, so backlog grows without additional control or capacity.
